verses.translation_literal: YHWH reigns; let peoples tremble. [He is] sitting [on] cherubim; let the earth quake.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is king. Let the nations shake at it! He sits enthroned upon the cherubim; let the whole earth reel beneath him.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is an enthronement shout, the same cry that opens Psalms 93, 96 and 97, but here the court is not cheering: it is bracing. Two short commands, each a pair of words, fall like blows: 'let them tremble', 'let it quake'. Play the second half of each line as the shudder that follows the first.

The KJV 'he sitteth between the cherubims' stretches the plural twice: 'cherubims' is a double plural (Hebrew already has -im), and 'between' is not in the Hebrew, which has only 'sitting [on] cherubim'. The picture is the winged guardian figures flanking the ark, whose lid was the throne in the Jerusalem temple, as Radak and Meiri say. The KJV also softens 'quake' to 'be moved': תָּנוּט is the verb of a shaken foundation, and Rashi ties it to 'my feet had almost slipped' (Ps 73:2). In the ancient Near East a king's accession meant the neighbours' nerves; this is the God version of it.

philological_notes.note: Tremble, shake, from fear or anger; the same verb as 'tremble and do not sin' in Ps 4:5. The shaking is a bodily reaction before a king.
A participle that works as a title, 'the one enthroned on the cherubim'. The cherubim are the winged figures over the ark, here named as his throne.
A rare verb, 'to totter, quake', found otherwise in Ps 17:5 (נָמוֹט, the cognate root מוט). Rashi links it to Ps 73:2.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH in Zion [is] great, and exalted [is] he over all the peoples.
verses.translation_dramatic: In Zion the LORD is great, and high above every people he rises, lifted beyond their reach.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tremor of verse 1 is answered with a location and a scale. Two adjectives, 'great' and 'exalted', cover two directions: great here in Zion, where he can be found, and high over everyone, where he cannot be reached. The word order puts YHWH first and Zion next, so the name and the city sit side by side; let the pause after 'Zion' hold.

The KJV 'above all the people' uses the singular for Hebrew 'peoples' (עַמִּים), which loses the plural that links this verse to v. 1; the BBE moves to 'nations'. The Hebrew is the same plural word as in v. 1. Zion is the temple hill in Jerusalem, so for the first audience this was a statement that the cosmic king has a fixed address, a claim neighbours would have heard as a challenge to their own city gods.

philological_notes.note: 'Great' and 'exalted'. Malbim distinguishes them: 'great' extends down to every worshipper in Zion, 'exalted' is the remoteness that nations feel. This is his reading, but the pairing of two adjectives is in the Hebrew.

verses.translation_literal: Let them give thanks [to] your name, great and feared: holy [is] he.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them praise your name, so great, so fearful. Holy is he.
verses.directors_commentary:
The shift from 'he' to 'you' is sudden: the psalm turns from describing the king to speaking to him. It is the 'peoples' of v. 1 who are told to give thanks, the same nations who were trembling; their fear becomes confession. The verse ends on the refrain 'holy is he', which returns in v. 5 and, expanded, in v. 9: three beats mark the psalm's three sections.

The KJV 'terrible name' is the classic archaism: נוֹרָא means 'to be feared, awe-inspiring', not 'dreadful' in the modern sense. The KJV also reads 'for it is holy', which makes the name the subject, while the Hebrew הוּא is 'he'; ASV and BBE are closer. And יוֹדוּ is not exactly 'praise': it is the verb of public acknowledgment, thanks that confesses something about the one thanked. Ibn Ezra remarks that 'name' here is the personal name revealed through Moses.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of ידה: to acknowledge publicly, to give thanks; with the object directly marked, 'give thanks to your name'. KJV 'praise' is looser.
Niphal participle of 'fear': 'one to be feared', awe-inspiring. KJV 'terrible' meant this in 1611.

verses.translation_literal: And [the] strength of [a] king, justice he loves. You, you established uprightness; justice and righteousness in Jacob, you, you have done.
verses.translation_dramatic: The might of a king, and it loves justice. You, and you alone, have set straightness in place; justice and righteousness in Jacob, it was you who made them.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse is the hinge of the psalm and its grammar is rough on purpose. The first clause is a fragment, almost a proverb: 'the strength of a king, justice he loves.' Then the speaker turns to God, and the pronoun 'you' lands twice, once before each verb. Play it as a person pointing: you, not the gods of the nations.

Two points the English versions blur. The KJV 'judgment' for מִשְׁפָּט is dated; it means 'justice, right order', and it appears twice here in two different positions, once as what the king loves and once as what God does in Jacob. And 'equity' for מֵישָׁרִים is a plural, 'straight things, evenness'; Rashi reads it as reconciliation between people, his example being the law to help your enemy's fallen donkey (Exod 23:4-5). In the ancient world a king's strength was proved by wars; here strength is defined by courts. Jacob is Israel as a people, in the Hebrew's older name.

philological_notes.note: A plural abstract, 'evenness, straightness, uprightness', used of fair dealing. Rashi reads it as peace-making between people.
'Justice and righteousness', a pair that sums up right government; Malbim distinguishes mishpat as what is deserved and tsedaqah as grace beyond what is deserved.

verses.translation_literal: Exalt YHWH our God, and bow down to [the] footstool of his feet: holy [is] he.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lift up the LORD our God! Bow yourselves low at the footstool of his feet. Holy is he.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first imperatives of the psalm: after 'let them', now 'you': the audience is addressed directly and the voice turns to 'our God'. 'Exalt' is the same root as 'exalted' in v. 2, so the people are asked to lift up the one who is already high; the echo is deliberate. The refrain 'holy is he' ends the section, as in v. 3.

The KJV 'worship at his footstool' is the usual rendering, but הִשְׁתַּחֲווּ means a physical act: to bow down, to prostrate oneself, and the preposition is 'to', not 'at'. The footstool is literal furniture, the low stool before a throne; Metzudat David and Radak identify it with the temple, and Ibn Ezra with the place of the ark. The enthroned king of v. 1 keeps his feet on this one spot of earth, so bowing means going to the ground before the ark.

philological_notes.note: The footstool of a throne; here a name for the temple or the ark, the earthly resting place of the heavenly king. Metzudat Zion compares Ps 110:1.
To bow down to the ground; a whole-body gesture of submission, not an inward attitude. The KJV 'worship' is the effect, not the act.

verses.translation_literal: Moses and Aaron [were] among his priests, and Samuel among those calling [on] his name; [they were] calling to YHWH, and he, he would answer them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Moses, and Aaron beside him, stood among his priests; and Samuel stood among those who call upon his name. They called out to the LORD, and again and again he answered them.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three names, and the audience knows every story behind them. Moses and Aaron come first, and the psalm calls them "priests": Aaron was the high priest, and Moses is called a priest because he officiated in the seven days of ordination (Lev 8), as Ibn Ezra and Radak both note. Samuel was no priest by office, so the poet gives him a second line, "among those who call on his name", the prayer-leaders. Ibn Ezra and Radak add that he came from the same line. In a world where a god's answer was sought through temple professionals, the psalm picks out three people whose cry was heard.

The KJV "they called upon the Lord, and he answered them" is fair, but it is one possible reading of the tenses. The participle "calling" sets a scene that goes on, and the verb "he answers" is an imperfect, which in this setting can mean "he would answer", a habit, or can be read as a simple past. KJV and ASV take the past; YLT's "doth answer" takes the present. All three are defensible. The literal layer keeps the habitual sense, and the dramatic layer follows it: not one answer but a pattern. Note the emphatic "and he, he" (וְהוּא): the answerer is set against the callers. The KJV's "Lord" for YHWH hides that the callers call to the personal name, which stands in the middle of the line.

Meiri and Metzudat David hear in the line also a warning: even these three needed forgiveness (Aaron at the calf, Moses and Aaron at Meribah, Samuel with his sons), and yet they were answered. That reading prepares the next verses.

philological_notes.note: 'Among his priests.' Moses is not called a priest elsewhere in the Torah narrative as a title, but he performed the priestly acts of the seven days of ordination. The psalm uses the broad sense: those who stand near and serve.

'He answers/would answer them.' An imperfect after participles: it can be habitual, so 'he would answer'; a simple past is also possible. The root ענה (answer) returns in verse 8 as 'you answered them' (עֲנִיתָם), tying the two verses together.
The spelling קֹרִאים keeps the aleph, which is silent. Radak says the aleph 'rests', as in חוטאים אל ה'; Meiri says it is an unusual form.

verses.translation_literal: In a pillar of cloud he speaks to them; they kept his testimonies, and a decree he gave to them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Out of a pillar of cloud he spoke to them. They kept his testimonies, and the statute he gave them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene is the wilderness: a tall column of cloud, and a voice that comes from inside it. The verbs move between 'he speaks' (a habit, a living voice) and 'they kept' (a finished record), as if the psalm were looking back on a closed chapter and still hearing it. Keep the cloud close and dark, and the voice calm.

The 'them' has no named antecedent. Ibn Ezra and Radak apply it to Moses and Aaron, since only to them does the Torah narrate speech from the cloud; Rashi and Meiri, quoting a midrash, add Samuel from 1 Sam 9:11-12. I leave the pronoun open. The KJV 'cloudy pillar' reverses the Hebrew order and turns the cloud into an adjective; the Hebrew is 'pillar of cloud' (עַמּוּד עָנָן), the phrase of Exod 33:9-10. KJV 'ordinance' for חֹק is a legal term from 1611; it is a 'decree', something engraved, a fixed rule. And 'testimonies' (עֵדוֹת) are the terms the covenant 'bears witness' to: the commandments.

philological_notes.note: 'His testimonies', the commandments seen as witness to the covenant; a common word in the psalms.
A decree or fixed rule; from 'to cut, engrave'. Singular here after a plural 'testimonies'.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH our God, you, you answered them; a God lifting [up sin] you were to them, and avenging upon their deeds.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD our God, it was you who answered them. A God who bore their guilt away, that is what you were to them, and yet you called their deeds to account.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the third-person narrative of verses 6-7, where Moses, Aaron and Samuel called and the LORD answered, the psalm returns to addressing God as "you", as it did in verses 3-4. The line is spoken to God's face, as a congregation's confession, and the pronoun אַתָּה is stated outright, which Hebrew does not need: "you, you answered them." Play it with weight on that pronoun.

The verse holds two things in tension: a God who forgives and a God who avenges. The KJV renders נֹשֵׂא as "forgavest", which is right in sense, but the word's root is "to lift, carry", the same verb used for a priest bearing guilt away. The KJV also turns the participles into a past "though thou tookest vengeance", which makes the vengeance a grudging exception. The Hebrew has no "though": it joins the two with a plain "and", and both are participles, which describe what God is like. BBE's "took away their sin" and "gave them punishment" is smoother but blurs the verb for avenging, נָקַם. KJV's "inventions" for עֲלִילוֹתָם is an archaic and narrow reading: the noun means deeds, what someone does, and here it is their misdeeds. Metzudat Zion ties it to the verb עולל, "to deal with someone".

The ancient readers disagreed on who the "them" are and what was avenged. Rashi and Metzudat David think of Moses and Aaron, who died outside the land because of Meribah (Num 20:10), and of Samuel, who is faulted for not guiding his sons (1 Sam 8:3). Ibn Ezra and Radak think of Korah and his party, the swallowed and the burned. Metzudat David draws the moral that God showed no favouritism even to the holiest. Actors should keep both readings open: the voice does not accuse, it marvels that the same God did both.

philological_notes.note: A participle of the verb 'to lift, carry', used with עָוֹן for bearing guilt, so 'forgiving' is literally 'lifting off'. The participle describes God's character, not one single act. Rashi supplies the object: the sin of Israel.
From עֲלִילָה, 'deed, doing', a neutral word that takes its colour from context. Here the deeds are wrongs that God took account of. Metzudat Zion links it to עולל, 'dealt with' (Lam 1:12).
The participle 'avenging' is joined to 'forgiving' by a bare 'and': the verse sets the two side by side without 'though'.

verses.translation_literal: Exalt YHWH our God, and bow down to [the] mountain of his holiness, for holy [is] YHWH our God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lift up the LORD our God! Bow down at his holy mountain, for holy is the LORD our God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm closes by repeating verse 5 almost word for word, and the one change is the point: 'his footstool' becomes 'his holy mountain', and the bare refrain 'holy is he' grows into 'holy is YHWH our God', now with the full name and 'our'. Say the last line slowly; it is the end of the song and the whole claim of the psalm, and the repetition of 'YHWH our God' from the first line of the verse gives it the sound of an echo.

The KJV 'holy hill' hides a small point: הַר קָדְשׁוֹ is literally 'the mountain of his holiness', a genitive and not an adjective, so holiness belongs to him and the hill borrows it. Radak and Metzudat David identify it with Mount Moriah and the temple. The ASV, KJV and BBE all read 'worship at' where the verb is again 'bow down to', and BBE's 'faces turned to' adds a direction the Hebrew lacks (though Ibn Ezra stresses that the bowing is to the God of the place, not to the place).

philological_notes.note: 'The mountain of his holiness': Zion or Moriah, the temple mount. The bound form makes holiness his own attribute.
